parts:
Hi,

there is nothing that does not exist :-) The parameter is fixed to zero and has no CI (because it is fixed). Zero is arbitrary but has the charm that the mean of the second group is equal to the mean difference (which is usually of interest). You can find a few additional notes here: https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/aptAZ5Gd-jI/m/xNlvu7DSAQAJ

Purely technically, you can do something like this:

library(lavaan)

HS.model.1 <- "
visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
textual ~ c(m1, m2) * 1
m1 == 0
"

fit.1 <- cfa(HS.model.1, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, group = "school", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))
pe.1 <- parameterEstimates(fit.1)
pe.1[pe.1$label == "m2", "est"]

HS.model.2 <- gsub("m1 == 0", paste0("m2", "==", pe.1[pe.1$label == "m2", "est"]), HS.model.1)          

fit.2 <- cfa(HS.model.2, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, group = "school", group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts"))
pe.2 <- parameterEstimates(fit.2)
pe.2[pe.2$label == "m1",]

Now you get a CI for the mean of group 1. However, the calculation as above is unnecessary, because you can also get the result this way:

round(pe.1[pe.1$label == "m2", "ci.lower"] - pe.1[pe.1$label == "m2", "est"], 3)
round(pe.1[pe.1$label == "m2", "ci.upper"] - pe.1[pe.1$label == "m2", "est"], 3) 


I can't provide a meaningful interpretation, because this CI doesn't contain any additional information. At least from my perspective. From a purely technical point of view, I hope that the code solves your problem?

parts:
If your goal is to compare the 7 means (one of them fixed to 0), you should not use CI overlap to do this.

Search overlap "confidence interval" and you will find some pages that explain why you should not do this.

The following example use a 3-group simple mediation model for illustration. The a-paths and the means of x1 in the three groups are compared in two ways:
- Compute the difference using user-defined parameters (":=").
- Check the CIs to see whether they overlap.

You can see that these two methods do not yield the same conclusion in some cases. In general, the power of the CI overlap method is lower than the direct test of the difference (explained mathematically in some of the pages that you can find from the search suggested above).

``` r
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-16
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
cov_list <- list(gp1 = lav_matrix_lower2full(c(1, .20, 1, .30, .06, 1)),
                 gp2 = lav_matrix_lower2full(c(1, .30, 1, .30, .09, 1)),
                 gp3 = lav_matrix_lower2full(c(1, .40, 1, .30, .12, 1)))
cov_list <- lapply(cov_list, function(x) {
    rownames(x) <- colnames(x) <- paste0("x", 1:3)
    x
  })
cov_list
#> $gp1
#>     x1   x2   x3
#> x1 1.0 0.20 0.30
#> x2 0.2 1.00 0.06
#> x3 0.3 0.06 1.00
#>
#> $gp2
#>     x1   x2   x3
#> x1 1.0 0.30 0.30
#> x2 0.3 1.00 0.09
#> x3 0.3 0.09 1.00
#>
#> $gp3
#>     x1   x2   x3
#> x1 1.0 0.40 0.30
#> x2 0.4 1.00 0.12
#> x3 0.3 0.12 1.00
mean_vec <- list(gp1 = c(x1 = .1, x2 = 0, x3 = 0),
                 gp2 = c(x1 = .2, x2 = 0, x3 = 0),
                 gp3 = c(x1 = .3, x2 = 0, x3 = 0))
mod <-
"
x2 ~ c(a1, a2, a3) * x1
x3 ~ x2 + x1
x1 ~ c(m1, m2, m3) * 1
a2a1 := a2 - a1
a3a2 := a3 - a2
a3a1 := a3 - a1
m2m1 := m2 - m1
m3m2 := m3 - m2
m3m1 := m3 - m1
"
n <- 1000
fit <- sem(mod,
           sample.nobs = c(n, n, n),
           sample.cov = cov_list,
           sample.mean = mean_vec,
           fixed.x = FALSE)
est <- parameterEstimates(fit)

# a path
est[((est$lhs == "x2") & (est$rhs == "x1")) | est$op == ":=", ][1:6, ]
#>     lhs op   rhs block group label est    se      z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 1    x2  ~    x1     1     1    a1 0.2 0.031  6.455  0.000    0.139    0.261
#> 10   x2  ~    x1     2     2    a2 0.3 0.030  9.945  0.000    0.241    0.359
#> 19   x2  ~    x1     3     3    a3 0.4 0.029 13.801  0.000    0.343    0.457
#> 28 a2a1 := a2-a1     0     0  a2a1 0.1 0.043  2.312  0.021    0.015    0.185
#> 29 a3a2 := a3-a2     0     0  a3a2 0.1 0.042  2.390  0.017    0.018    0.182
#> 30 a3a1 := a3-a1     0     0  a3a1 0.2 0.042  4.714  0.000    0.117    0.283
# Compare CIs:
# a1 vs. a2: Overlap?
est[1, "ci.upper"] > est[10, "ci.lower"]
#> [1] TRUE
# a2 vs. a3: Overlap?
est[10, "ci.upper"] > est[19, "ci.lower"]
#> [1] TRUE
# a1 vs. a3: Overlap?
est[1, "ci.upper"] > est[19, "ci.lower"]
#> [1] FALSE

# Mean of x1
est[((est$lhs == "x1") & (est$op == "~1")) | est$op == ":=", ][-c(4:6), ]
#>     lhs op   rhs block group label est    se     z pvalue ci.lower ci.upper
#> 4    x1 ~1           1     1    m1 0.1 0.032 3.164  0.002    0.038    0.162
#> 13   x1 ~1           2     2    m2 0.2 0.032 6.328  0.000    0.138    0.262
#> 22   x1 ~1           3     3    m3 0.3 0.032 9.492  0.000    0.238    0.362
#> 31 m2m1 := m2-m1     0     0  m2m1 0.1 0.045 2.237  0.025    0.012    0.188
#> 32 m3m2 := m3-m2     0     0  m3m2 0.1 0.045 2.237  0.025    0.012    0.188
#> 33 m3m1 := m3-m1     0     0  m3m1 0.2 0.045 4.474  0.000    0.112    0.288
# Compare CIs:
# m1 vs. m2: Overlap?
est[4, "ci.upper"] > est[13, "ci.lower"]
#> [1] TRUE
# m2 vs. m3: Overlap?
est[13, "ci.upper"] > est[22, "ci.lower"]
#> [1] TRUE
# m1 vs. m3: Overlap?
est[4, "ci.upper"] > est[22, "ci.lower"]
#> [1] FALSE
```

library(lavaan)

As already explained in previous post, with the latent mean of one group (1st group by default) fixed to zero, the other means can be interpreted as the difference in means compared to the reference group. However, with three groups, we need to manually define the difference (m3m2 := m3 - m2). As illustrated above, the SE and pvalue (0.082, .014) are exactly identical to those of the "mean" of the 3rd group (m3 in fit2) by setting the 2nd group as the reference group. This is expected, because this mean of the 3rd group is still a mean difference, but compared to the 2nd group in fit2.

This example also illustrates why CI overlap should not be used. In fit1, with 1st group as the reference group, CIs for the 2nd group and the 3rd group are available, and overlap (-0.059-0.259 vs. 0.139 -0.461). However, both the self-computed difference (m3m2 := m3 - m2) and the alternative model (fit2) show that the latent means of the 2nd and 3rd groups are significantly different.

Therefore, with 7 groups, if necessary, we can do pairwise comparison using only one model, and compute the difference as shown above. Certainly, just like an usual ANOVA, there is a risk of Type I error inflation in these (post hoc?) comparison. Some methods need to be used to control the Type I error rate.

My two cents.

-- Shu Fai

As already explained in previous post, with the latent mean of one group (1st group by default) fixed to zero, the other means can be interpreted as the difference in means compared to the reference group. However, with three groups, we need to manually define the difference (m3m2 := m3 - m2). As illustrated above, the SE and pvalue (0.082, .014) are exactly identical to those of the "mean" of the 3rd group (m3 in fit2) by setting the 2nd group as the reference group. This is expected, because this mean of the 3rd group is still a mean difference, but compared to the 2nd group in fit2.

This example also illustrates why CI overlap should not be used. In fit1, with 1st group as the reference group, CIs for the 2nd group and the 3rd group are available, and overlap (-0.059-0.259 vs. 0.139 -0.461). However, both the self-computed difference (m3m2 := m3 - m2) and the alternative model (fit2) show that the latent means of the 2nd and 3rd groups are significantly different.

Therefore, with 7 groups, if necessary, we can do pairwise comparison using only one model, and compute the difference as shown above. Certainly, just like an usual ANOVA, there is a risk of Type I error inflation in these (post hoc?) comparison. Some methods need to be used to control the Type I error rate.

My two cents.

-- Shu Fai

Thanks, Christian. This is an interesting technique. The source is this one:

Tryon, W. W. (2001). Evaluating statistical difference, equivalence, and indeterminacy using inferential confidence intervals: An integrated alternative method of conducting null hypothesis statistical tests. Psychological Methods, 6(4), 371–386. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.6.4.371

The value "84%" actually came (indirectly) from Goldstein and Healy (1995), which Tryon cited (see Footnote 3 of Tryon). (I haven't read Tryon in detail ... Tryon proposed an extension of the method by Goldstein and Healy to t test , when sample size is finite [not "large"], as far as I understand.)

Goldstein, H., & Healy, M. J. R. (1995). The graphical presentation of a collection of means. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series A (Statistics in Society), 158(1), 175. https://doi.org/10.2307/2983411

Interestingly, Goldstein and Healy (1995) wrote, in the first paragraph, "It is a common statistical misconception to suppose that two quantities whose 95% confidence intervals just fail to overlap are significantly different at the 5% level." They mentioned a solution: making the CIs of means narrower such that using CI overlap and testing the difference (using large sample z test, in the 1995 paper) yield identical conclusion. The 84% CIs can indeed achieve this goal, with one assumption: the standard errors for both means are the same.

(I am not sure whether they proposed that solution because this was mentioned in the 1st paragraph. The method they focused on is for a more complicated scenario. That 84% solution is not their main interest.)

This leads to two issues.

First, the value 84% is usually inappropriate because the standard errors of the two means are not necessarily equal, especially in SEM and CFA, unless the SEs are made equal, usually unintentionally, due to some model constrains. Goldstein and Healy should be aware of the limitations of this assumption (in other contexts) and what they proposed later in the paper does not rely on this assumption.

Second, the CI overlap method using adjusted CIs does not replace the direct test on the difference in means nor performs better than the direct test. The CI overlap method is designed to be equivalent to the direct test, at least under some conditions. (Goldstein and Healy, as well as Tryon, proposed the adjusted CI methods mainly for facilitating the visualization of means, as far as I understand).
So, in my personal opinion, if the goal is to compare means, then testing the differences directly is enough. The CI overlap method with adjusted CIs can be used in addition to, rather than in place of, the tests of the differences, unless it is certain that the two methods yield identical conclusions.

My two cents.

-- Shu Fai

As already explained in previous post, with the latent mean of one group (1st group by default) fixed to zero, the other means can be interpreted as the difference in means compared to the reference group. However, with three groups, we need to manually define the difference (m3m2 := m3 - m2). As illustrated above, the SE and pvalue (0.082, .014) are exactly identical to those of the "mean" of the 3rd group (m3 in fit2) by setting the 2nd group as the reference group. This is expected, because this mean of the 3rd group is still a mean difference, but compared to the 2nd group in fit2.

This example also illustrates why CI overlap should not be used. In fit1, with 1st group as the reference group, CIs for the 2nd group and the 3rd group are available, and overlap (-0.059-0.259 vs. 0.139 -0.461). However, both the self-computed difference (m3m2 := m3 - m2) and the alternative model (fit2) show that the latent means of the 2nd and 3rd groups are significantly different.

Therefore, with 7 groups, if necessary, we can do pairwise comparison using only one model, and compute the difference as shown above. Certainly, just like an usual ANOVA, there is a risk of Type I error inflation in these (post hoc?) comparison. Some methods need to be used to control the Type I error rate.

My two cents.

-- Shu Fai

Thanks, Christian. This is an interesting technique. The source is this one:

Tryon, W. W. (2001). Evaluating statistical difference, equivalence, and indeterminacy using inferential confidence intervals: An integrated alternative method of conducting null hypothesis statistical tests. Psychological Methods, 6(4), 371–386. https://doi.org/10.1037/1082-989X.6.4.371

The value "84%" actually came (indirectly) from Goldstein and Healy (1995), which Tryon cited (see Footnote 3 of Tryon). (I haven't read Tryon in detail ... Tryon proposed an extension of the method by Goldstein and Healy to t test , when sample size is finite [not "large"], as far as I understand.)

Goldstein, H., & Healy, M. J. R. (1995). The graphical presentation of a collection of means. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series A (Statistics in Society), 158(1), 175. https://doi.org/10.2307/2983411

Interestingly, Goldstein and Healy (1995) wrote, in the first paragraph, "It is a common statistical misconception to suppose that two quantities whose 95% confidence intervals just fail to overlap are significantly different at the 5% level." They mentioned a solution: making the CIs of means narrower such that using CI overlap and testing the difference (using large sample z test, in the 1995 paper) yield identical conclusion. The 84% CIs can indeed achieve this goal, with one assumption: the standard errors for both means are the same.

(I am not sure whether they proposed that solution because this was mentioned in the 1st paragraph. The method they focused on is for a more complicated scenario. That 84% solution is not their main interest.)

This leads to two issues.

First, the value 84% is usually inappropriate because the standard errors of the two means are not necessarily equal, especially in SEM and CFA, unless the SEs are made equal, usually unintentionally, due to some model constrains. Goldstein and Healy should be aware of the limitations of this assumption (in other contexts) and what they proposed later in the paper does not rely on this assumption.

Second, the CI overlap method using adjusted CIs does not replace the direct test on the difference in means nor performs better than the direct test. The CI overlap method is designed to be equivalent to the direct test, at least under some conditions. (Goldstein and Healy, as well as Tryon, proposed the adjusted CI methods mainly for facilitating the visualization of means, as far as I understand).
So, in my personal opinion, if the goal is to compare means, then testing the differences directly is enough. The CI overlap method with adjusted CIs can be used in addition to, rather than in place of, the tests of the differences, unless it is certain that the two methods yield identical conclusions.

My two cents.

-- Shu Fai

As already explained in previous post, with the latent mean of one group (1st group by default) fixed to zero, the other means can be interpreted as the difference in means compared to the reference group. However, with three groups, we need to manually define the difference (m3m2 := m3 - m2). As illustrated above, the SE and pvalue (0.082, .014) are exactly identical to those of the "mean" of the 3rd group (m3 in fit2) by setting the 2nd group as the reference group. This is expected, because this mean of the 3rd group is still a mean difference, but compared to the 2nd group in fit2.

This example also illustrates why CI overlap should not be used. In fit1, with 1st group as the reference group, CIs for the 2nd group and the 3rd group are available, and overlap (-0.059-0.259 vs. 0.139 -0.461). However, both the self-computed difference (m3m2 := m3 - m2) and the alternative model (fit2) show that the latent means of the 2nd and 3rd groups are significantly different.

Therefore, with 7 groups, if necessary, we can do pairwise comparison using only one model, and compute the difference as shown above. Certainly, just like an usual ANOVA, there is a risk of Type I error inflation in these (post hoc?) comparison. Some methods need to be used to control the Type I error rate.

My two cents.

Shu Fai wrote:
>Some methods need to be used to control the Type I error rate.

Juli, Rather than something like a Bonferoni procedure that may result in excessively low power, you might consider another option which is to conduct "protected tests" as described in the regression book by Cohen, Cohen, West & Aiken.  First test that all the means are equal using a chi-square difference test.  If you fail to reject that hypothesis, then stop and conduct no more tests (this is the protected par).  If you do reject this hypothesis, then interpret that as an omnibus test indicating that there is at least one difference and conduct the pairwise tests described by Shu Fai without any further adjustments.

Currently that is my preferred approach but I would of course be interested to know if others are aware of a preferable option.

Keith

Hi Christian,
I am not a statistician.  However, here is the way I think about it.  The assumption of perfect fit of the nesting model applies to the population, not the sample.  So imperfect fit in the sample does not necessarily indicate violation of the assumption if it is within sampling error.  If the fit is within reason and this is not one of the primary hypotheses for the study, I might be inclined to just go with the protected test (for the same reason that we typically go with the z tests rather than setting up a chi-square difference for every parameter in the model).  If the fit is within reason and the hypothesis is a central focus of the study, then I might invest in the resampling approach as you suggested.  If the fit is very bad, then I am not sure that I would trust the estimates enough to even trust the resampling approach.  In that case, I would focus on re-specifying the nesting model.  It might be an interesting area for some simulation work.  Perhaps others have additional thoughts.
